newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coupmakers seek deal, firm on terms.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coupmakers seek deal, firm on terms.

text.p: Sierra Leone's coupmakers and their rebel allies say they want a negotiated settlement to their standoff with regional giant Nigeria but will not reinstate toppled civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

Andrew Koroma, secretary-general of their Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), told Reuters on Thursday that they had sent envoys to Ivory Coast to ask its president, Henri Konan Bedie, to intervene to break the deadlock.
But he said that they stood by their earlier rejection to reinstate Kabbah, though they were prepared to organise elections within 18 months to two years.
Freetown, flooded with rebel fighters since the May 25 coup, was calm on Friday, with residents saying they hoped for a negotiated settlement to the crisis.

Sierra Leone's chief of defence staff Brigadier Samuel Koroma told a Thursday news conference they had sent a message to Nigerian military leader General Sani Abacha via a delegation he sent to talk to them.
"We have sent a message...saying that General Abacha must choose between peace in Sierra Leone or the forced return of president Kabbah to power by Nigeria and ECOMOG," he said.
Nigeria, which already had troops of the West African ECOMOG force in Freetown under a defence agreement, has been steadily reinforcing in the city since the coup.

"We are not prepared to hand over to former president Kabbah," the chief of defence staff said. "If president Kabbah takes over again, he will jeopardise the peace that we have been able to achieve with the RUF rebels."
Foday Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front has been fighting a bush war since 1991. A peace accord signed with Kabbah last November failed to hold, and the rebels have joined the coup.
Coup leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah named Sankoh vice-chairman in his Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC).
AFRC secretary-general Koroma told Reuters a six-man delegation led by Sierra Leone's ambassador to Guinea, Colonel Mohamed Diaby, had left for Ivory Coast.
The aim, he said, was to ask Bedie "to step in to resolve the present impasse between between the AFRC and ECOMOG in order to resolve this situation by negotiations and not by armed confrontation."
Bedie helped broker a fragile peace in Sierra Leone last year. Diaby was kidnapped by rebels in the east in March and only freed after the coup.
Nigerian gunboats shelled Freetown on Monday in a show of force. Rebels attacked Nigerian troops guarding foreigners. The United States, France and other countries evacuated nationals.

Brigadier Koroma said if Nigerian-led forces restored Kabbah to power the military would overthrow him again, but he promised the AFRC would organise elections within two years "for the people to choose the leader they want".
Local politicians have rejected that idea out of hand.

The impoverished, war-torn country's third coup in five years has been condemned at home and abroad. The Organisation of African Unity summit, which ended in Harare on Wednesday, called for restoration of Kabbah, who was elected in March 1996 after four years of army rule. He is now in neighbouring Guinea.
Thousands of people have fled the capital for the provinces. The military say 80 people were killed on Monday, other sources put the toll at fewer than 50.
